n: Not found in Genesis: God tells Moses that the Satan he cast out is the same being who, before the world, offered to be God’s son and redeem everyone so no soul would be lost—demanding God’s honor in return.

f.w: that one soul shall not be lost
f.g: Satan’s plan sounds generous but would require removing choice.

n: In contrast, the Beloved Son—chosen from the beginning—said, “Father, thy will be done, and the glory be thine forever.” Christ sought the Father’s glory, not his own.
Satan rebelled, sought to destroy human agency, and wanted God’s own power. By the power of the Only Begotten, God cast him down. This premortal “war in heaven” centered on agency.

f.w: sought to destroy the agency of man

f.g: The God-given ability and freedom to choose and act for oneself.

n: He became Satan (“adversary”) and the devil, father of lies, who deceives, blinds, and enslaves all who won’t listen to God.
Now the story returns to Eden. The serpent was more cunning than any other animal.

Moses clarifies that Satan worked through the serpent. He sought to deceive Eve because he did not understand God’s plan; he meant to destroy the world, not realizing the Fall was part of God’s design.

f.w: he knew not the mind of God
f.g: Satan’s ignorance of God’s plan: the Fall he engineered actually opened the way to redemption.

n: Satan begins with a question twisting God’s words: “Did God really say you can’t eat from every tree?”
Eve answers that they may eat of the trees of the garden.

f.w: We may eat of the fruit of the trees

n: But not of the tree in the middle—they must not eat or even touch it, or they will die.

f.g: Eve’s report adds “touch,” which is not in God’s recorded command.

n: The serpent flatly contradicts God: “Ye shall not surely die.” This mixes truth and lie—they would not die immediately, but they would become mortal.
He claims God is withholding something: eating will open their eyes and make them like gods, knowing good and evil. Part of this was true, which made the deception powerful.

f.w: ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil

n: Eve saw the fruit was good, beautiful, and desirable for wisdom; she ate and gave some to Adam. Latter-day Saints view their choice as a necessary step that made mortal life and progress possible.

f.w: a tree to be desired to make her wise

n: Their eyes opened; they realized they were naked and made aprons of fig leaves. Innocence was replaced by awareness.

f.w: they knew that they had been naked

n: Hearing God in the garden in the cool of the day, they hid among the trees. Sin brings the impulse to hide from God.

f.w: in the cool of the day
f.g: Literally “the wind of the day,” likely evening breezes.

n: God calls, “Where goest thou?”—not because he doesn’t know, but to invite Adam to account for himself. (Genesis reads “Where art thou?”)
Adam admits he heard God, was afraid because he was naked, and hid.
God asks who told him he was naked, and whether he ate from the forbidden tree.

f.w: Who told thee thou wast naked?

n: Adam explains that the woman God gave him—and commanded to stay with him—gave him the fruit. Moses adds that God had commanded Eve to remain with Adam, which helps explain his choice.

f.w: commandest that she should remain with me
f.g: A Moses addition not in Genesis.

n: God asks Eve what she has done; she answers honestly that the serpent deceived her.
The serpent is cursed to crawl and eat dust—a symbol of humiliation and defeat.

f.w: upon thy belly shalt thou go

n: God puts hostility between the serpent and the woman, and their offspring. Her “seed” will crush the serpent’s head while the serpent bruises his heel—understood as the first prophecy of Christ’s victory over Satan.

f.w: he shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel
f.g: A heel wound is painful but survivable; a head wound is fatal.

n: Eve will experience pain and sorrow in childbirth. The phrase about her husband ruling has been explained by Church leaders in terms of loving, presiding partnership rather than domination.

f.w: In sorrow thou shalt bring forth children

f.g: Some modern Church teachings suggest “rule with” as a better sense, stressing equal partnership.

n: Because Adam ate, the ground is cursed “for thy sake”—for his benefit. Hard work would help him grow.

f.w: cursed shall be the ground for thy sake
f.g: “For thy sake” suggests the hardship is for Adam’s good.

n: Thorns and thistles will grow; Adam will eat plants of the field.
He will earn bread by sweat until death returns him to the dust from which he came. Mortality and toil are now part of life.

f.w: By the sweat of thy face

n: Adam names his wife Eve, “mother of all living.” Like Adam, her name represents many.

f.g: Hebrew Chavvah, related to the word for “living.”

n: God makes garments of skins and clothes them—a tender act of care, and for many readers a symbol of Christ’s covering atonement, since it required a sacrifice.
God tells the Only Begotten that man now knows good and evil, and must not eat from the tree of life and live forever in his sins.

f.w: lest he put forth his hand and partake also of the tree of life

n: So God sends Adam out of Eden to farm the ground he came from.
God’s words cannot return empty; they must be fulfilled—the warned consequence of death must happen.
God drove them out and placed cherubim and a flaming sword east of Eden to guard the tree of life. This gave Adam and Eve time to repent—a “probationary state.”

f.g: Heavenly guardian beings; also depicted on the ark of the covenant.

f.w: keep the way of the tree of life

n: A closing note: these are the words God spoke to Moses, now given to Joseph Smith, to be shared only with believers for the time being.
